steps.title: What is ‘Space Science’?
steps.heading: Scientific investigation about, or conducted within, the space environment

builds.point: A broad definition, taking in many fields, with approaches in common.
The topic drives the science, not the circumstances: we once studied Mars through telescopes, now we do robotic fieldwork with rovers.

callout.caption: Our researchers were on the NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return Campaign Science Group and worked on planetary protection, planning how best to bring Perseverance’s Jezero Crater samples to Earth and analyse them.

builds.point: Motivations range from the origins of the Universe to how materials behave in space.

steps.title: Going into space is only part of the picture
steps.heading: Going into space is only part of the picture
points: It might be a key part of any study, but it is never the whole story.

callout.caption: Part of our teaching, the Mars Yard lets students drive robotic rovers across a simulated Martian landscape from their own homes, making space science hands-on for learners anywhere.

builds.point: Atmospheric density drops with altitude.
Near space, the gas tends to be atomic and ionised rather than molecular: a plasma.
Hydrogen and helium come from the solar wind.

steps.title: The atmosphere blocks some wavelengths
steps.heading: The atmosphere blocks certain wavelengths of light

builds.title: Visible light and radio reach the ground

builds.point: At 250 km the gas density and radiation are unlike anything at the Earth’s surface.

steps.title: The magnetic field, dust and debris
steps.heading: The local space environment

builds.point: The Earth’s magnetic field has a strong effect on how charged particles move.
There is solid material too: dust grains, and space debris.
Buoyancy can take balloons to about 30 km.

callout.caption: A scientific balloon, about 30 km up.

steps.title: Sounding rockets: several hundred km, sub-orbital
steps.heading: Reaching the space environment
points: Sounding rockets reach several hundred km, but are sub-orbital.

callout.caption: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) characterises and optimises the four EM-CCD sensors in OGRE’s X-ray camera, built by the UK company XCAM to survive the violent vibrations of launch.

steps.title: Low Earth orbit
steps.heading: Reaching the space environment
points: Larger rockets are needed to reach low Earth orbit (LEO).

callout.caption: Our scientists took part in BIOMEX, a DLR-led experiment outside the ISS that exposed bacteria, algae, lichens and fungi to the vacuum, UV radiation and temperature extremes of space for about 18 months.

steps.title: Beyond LEO: GEO, the Moon, L1 and L2
steps.heading: Reaching the space environment
points: Further propulsion takes craft beyond LEO: to geostationary orbit, the Moon, L1 and L2.

steps.title: Swing-bys to the outer planets
steps.heading: Reaching the space environment
points: Planetary swing-by manoeuvres make interplanetary journeys possible.

builds.title: JUICE’s cruise: a week a second

callout.caption: Working with Teledyne e2v, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) helped develop and characterise the CIS115 sensor at the heart of the JANUS camera, testing it against the radiation, vibration and temperature extremes of the journey to Jupiter.

builds.point: Payload: the science instruments (cameras, telescopes, particle detectors…).

callout.caption: The primary mirror: 18 gold-coated beryllium segments, 6.5 m across.

builds.point: Systems: power, thermal control, attitude and orbit control, data handling, communications, control, structure.

callout.caption: Thermal control: the sunshield keeps the telescope below 50 K.

steps.heading: Fields within space science
points: Space plasma physics
Solar physics
Planetary sciences
Earth-observation science

Space technology

builds.point: The Earth’s magnetic field shapes the near-space environment: the magnetosphere.
The solar wind, a constant outflow of plasma from the Sun, carries the Sun’s magnetic field out into space.

callout.caption: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) developed and tested the twin CCD370 detectors (4,510 × 4,510 pixels, derived from the CCD270s developed for PLATO) at the heart of SMILE’s Soft X-ray Imager.

steps.title: 28 October 2003: a coronal mass ejection
steps.heading: Space plasma physics
points: Energetic solar events send denser plasma into the magnetosphere.

builds.title: A CME leaves the Sun at 2,100 km/s

steps.title: The storm reaches Earth
steps.heading: Space plasma physics
points: The field is fairly steady but the plasma flow is highly variable: the magnetosphere is dynamic.

builds.point: Geomagnetic storms bring aurorae, disrupt satellite and aircraft communications, and surge power lines.

steps.title: Space weather: the aurora, far south
steps.heading: Space weather
points: Space weather is important to monitor: in-situ measurements of magnetic fields and particle fluxes.

builds.point: The Sun is the only star we can study close up.

callout.caption: The Sun in extreme ultraviolet.

builds.point: Its overall output is steady, but in X-rays, UV and radio it is highly variable: magnetic activity in the photosphere.
Activity has an 11-year cycle (in fact a 22-year cycle of the global field).
Solar activity drives space weather. From space we can watch constantly, in X-rays and UV, at high resolution.

steps.title: Planetary sciences
steps.heading: Planetary sciences
points: Planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, meteorites and dust.

builds.point: Geology, mineralogy, atmospheric and magnetospheric physics, celestial mechanics, and astrobiology.

callout.caption: Our academics are on Curiosity’s science and operations teams, focusing on noble gases and on how Martian rocks reacted with ancient water, which bears on whether Mars was habitable.

steps.title: The Moon
steps.heading: Planetary sciences
points: Techniques: imaging, spectroscopy, radar, laser altimetry, particle detectors…

callout.caption: In April 2025 we became one of only seven institutions outside China chosen to borrow Chang’e-5 samples.
We’re developing EMS-L, the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer for LUPEX, an ESA instrument on the JAXA-ISRO rover.

steps.title: Comets: Rosetta and Philae
steps.heading: Planetary sciences
points: Motivations: explaining what we see, how planets evolve, the origin of the Solar System, resources.

callout.caption: With RAL Space, we co-developed Ptolemy, the gas analyser on the Philae lander that measured the isotopes of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen in the comet.
With RAL Space, we designed and built the Ptolemy gas analyser, which with the COSAC instrument made the first analysis of organic matter on a comet’s surface.

steps.title: Astrobiology: Enceladus
steps.heading: Astrobiology
points: One of our planetary scientists sat on ESA’s Expert Committee that, in 2024, recommended Enceladus as the target of ESA’s next large mission: an orbiter and lander to search for signs of life, for launch in the early 2040s.

callout.caption: Our planetary scientists use Cassini’s datasets to study the habitability and chemistry of Saturn’s icy moons.

builds.point: From space we can monitor the atmosphere, land, oceans and ice, constantly and on a large scale.

callout.caption: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) tests how radiation damages the Teledyne e2v CIS120 CMOS sensor, which is being evaluated for TRUTHS and other next-generation missions.

builds.point: The techniques are like planetary science’s, but here we can do fieldwork to find the ‘ground truth’.
Drivers: weather, climate, resource planning, defence.
The atmosphere is opaque to gamma rays, X-rays, hard UV, and mid and far infrared.
It also blurs ground-based images and adds noise to measurements of brightness.

steps.title: Observatories: Hubble
steps.heading: Space-based astronomy
points: Observatories: Hubble, Spitzer, XMM-Newton, Chandra; JWST.

steps.title: What Hubble sees: a light echo
steps.heading: Space-based astronomy

callout.caption: Our astronomers use Hubble’s archive to study stellar populations and how distant galaxies evolve, and the work feeds into our astronomy teaching.
Our astronomers use JWST to study the atmospheres of planets around other stars.

steps.title: All-sky surveys: Gaia and Planck
steps.heading: Space-based astronomy
points: All-sky surveys: ROSAT, Hipparcos, Gaia, Planck.

builds.title: How the Milky Way’s stars move (Gaia)

callout.caption: Before launch, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) modelled how radiation damage would trap charge in Gaia’s CCDs, and we’ve since analysed its in-flight radiation data for the mission’s data processing.

builds.point: Novel instruments: the evolution of detectors for X-rays and light.

callout.caption: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) played a lead role in characterising the CCD273 detectors in Euclid’s VIS instrument, and developed ‘trap pumping’, now used in orbit.

builds.point: Human spaceflight; robotic and semi-autonomous control; propulsion, power and thermal control.
Communications, and data management and products.

callout.caption: Our Compact CMOS Camera Demonstrator (C3D) won one of only three science payload slots on UKube-1, the UK Space Agency’s first CubeSat.
